newsitem.title: UK: Copper to fall in 1997, but others upbeat - Wolff.
newsitem.headline: Copper to fall in 1997, but others upbeat - Wolff.

text.p: Global demand growth of four percent will underpin all base metal prices in 1997, with the exception of oversupplied copper, London Metal Exchange (LME) broker Rudolf Wolff and Co said.

In a special report on the metals market, Wolff analysts William Adams and Martin Squires said that the overriding factor supporting a stronger global economy in 1997 was that inventory adjustments are believed to be drawing to a close.
This "should lead to re-stocking and strong demand in the major economies," Wolff said.

Looking at the individual metals, Wolff said that copper will remain volatile during the rest of this year, but will eventually trend lower as mined production rises 760,000 tonnes this year and another 500,000 tonnes in 1997.
"This, coupled with an increase in smelter capacity and the resultant rise in refined production, is expected to lead to a combined surplus of some 557,000 tonnes over 1996 and 1997," Wolff said.
With a further surplus likely in 1998 prices were likely to remain depressed over the next couple of years, falling to $1,600 and averaging $1,750 in 1997.
Aluminium production is expected to rise significantly this year, due to South Africa's Alusaf smelter reaching full capacity and some post-MOU restarts.
However, with demand seen rising four percent in 1997 prices should recover, Wolff said.
Zinc prices will also recover strongly in 1997, underpinned by total commercial stocks dropping from around 8.6 weeks of consumption to a critical six weeks and resulting in a supply deficit.
Demand, flat this year, is seen rising by 3.5 percent next year with non-OECD countries continuing to gain market share.
Lead prices should post further gains in 1997, as consumption rises by four percent, underpinned by the replacement battery sector and low commercial stocks.
Nickel consumption is forecast growing strongly by 4.5 percent, while there is insufficient new production coming on-stream in the next couple of years.
Meanwhile, tin's supply deficit is set to grow in 1997 which will lead to a further drawdown in stocks, Wolff said.
Wolff forecasts for 1997, basis London Metal Exchange three months delivery prices, were as follows in $/tonne:
Aluminium 1,750 1,563
Lead 820 789
